reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A terminal deletion of the long arm of chromosome 11 (11q23 to the telomere), usually de novo and of variable size
Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia is characteristic: a constitutional platelet disorder with reduced numbers and impaired function, causing a lifelong bleeding tendency
Congenital heart disease is common, often involving left-sided lesions such as hypoplastic left heart, as well as septal defects
Trigonocephaly with a prominent metopic ridge is a recognisable craniofacial feature
Developmental delay and intellectual disability of variable degree, frequently with attention and behavioural difficulties
Additional features include feeding difficulty, recurrent infection, and eye, kidney and gastrointestinal anomalies
Haploinsufficiency of FLI1 is implicated in the platelet phenotype
Chromosomal microarray defines the deletion and its extent; a bleeding history warrants haematology involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Jacobsen syndrome is caused by loss of the terminal long arm of chromosome 11, most often as a de novo terminal deletion of variable size, with some cases arising from an unbalanced parental translocation. It is a contiguous-gene disorder in which haploinsufficiency of multiple dosage-sensitive genes produces the multisystem phenotype. Loss of FLI1, a transcription factor required for normal megakaryocyte and platelet development, underlies the Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia, while loss of other genes contributes to the cardiac, craniofacial and neurodevelopmental features. Larger deletions tend to be associated with more extensive involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Other terminal deletion or contiguous-gene syndromes with congenital heart disease and developmental delay
Inherited thrombocytopenias and platelet-function disorders from other causes
Other syndromic causes of trigonocephaly and metopic synostosis
Unbalanced products of a parental chromosomal rearrangement
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray as the first-line test to detect and size the terminal deletion
FISH or MLPA to confirm the deletion and assess for a parental rearrangement
Parental karyotype and studies to exclude a balanced translocation with recurrence implications
Full blood count and platelet studies to characterise the thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction
Echocardiography to define congenital heart disease
Renal, ophthalmological and developmental assessment; brain and other imaging as indicated
redFlags: Significant bleeding or the need for surgery in a child with the platelet disorder
Faltering growth or severe feeding difficulty in infancy
Recurrent or severe infection suggesting immune involvement
reference.prognosis: Outlook is largely determined by the severity of the congenital heart disease and the bleeding tendency, both of which are important early causes of morbidity; the thrombocytopenia persists lifelong and requires bleeding precautions, particularly around surgery. With cardiac correction and appropriate developmental support, many children survive into adulthood with variable intellectual disability.
pitfalls: Overlooking the constitutional platelet disorder and failing to take bleeding precautions before procedures or surgery
Omitting echocardiography given the high frequency of serious congenital heart disease
Failing to arrange parental studies to identify an inherited translocation with recurrence implications
Attributing the thrombocytopenia to an acquired cause and missing its constitutional Paris-Trousseau nature
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Bleeding precautions for Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia, with platelet transfusion cover around surgery and avoidance of antiplatelet drugs
Cardiology assessment and surgical correction of congenital heart disease, frequently left-sided lesions and septal defects
Early developmental support with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and tailored educational intervention for intellectual disability
Management of recurrent infection with immune evaluation, and feeding support for feeding difficulties
Surveillance and management of associated renal, ophthalmological and gastrointestinal anomalies
Genetic counselling with parental karyotype and studies to assess recurrence risk from a balanced translocation
Multidisciplinary follow-up coordinating cardiac, haematological and developmental care
